It solves the problem of temporal color bleeding artifacts caused by high correlation between RGB channels, which leads to poorly aligned bounding boxes and stale color information persisting across frames [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that performing history rectification in RGB space causes artifacts because RGB channels are highly correlated, leading to poorly aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) with the actual distribution of color samples. It further explains that transforming to luminance-chrominance spaces (like YCoCg or YCrCb) solves this by orienting the bounding box in the direction of luma, which reduces color-related ghosting/bleeding artifacts. The evidence also confirms that high correlation in RGB leads to stale color information persisting across frames (temporal color bleeding).
supported

- **Color-Related Artifacts in RGB:** Performing history rectification directly in RGB space causes the AABB to be poorly aligned with the actual distribution of color samples because RGB channels are highly correlated, leading to ghosting artifacts [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that performing history rectification directly in RGB space causes the AABB to be poorly aligned with the actual distribution of color samples because RGB channels are highly correlated, leading to ghosting artifacts. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms this: 'Performing history rectification directly in RGB color space can produce colorrelated artifacts since the RGB channels are commonly highly correlated. As seen in Figure 2.10 (a), the RGB-space AABB can become poorly aligned with the actual distribution of color samples.' It further explains that transforming to luminance-chrominance spaces orients the bounding box in the direction of luma, resulting in 'fewer color-related ghosting artifacts,' which supports the claim that RGB space leads to such artifacts due to poor alignment.
